title: Does Your Reasoning Model Implicitly Know When to Stop Thinking?
claim: Our RL training scheme mixes efficient samples into rollouts, improving accuracy while using substantially fewer tokens across many benchmarks.
layout: 2 stacked sections: pipeline diagram on top, two radar charts below
description: The figure has two stacked parts inside a dashed border. The top, labeled SAGE-RL on the left in a grey band, is a small pipeline diagram. Input x feeds a yellow Policy Model, which produces a group of rollouts (y^r and y^s, in light blue and teal). These go to Reference Model and Verifiable Rewards boxes, producing rewards r^r and r^s. The rewards go to an RLVR Baseline box and then to advantage A, which loops back to the policy. Below it, a teal banner says SAGE-RL enables LRMs to learn efficient reasoning patterns. A six-color legend sits under the banner, with dashed lines for base models and solid lines for SAGE-GRPO models. Two radar charts follow. The left one shows accuracy on six math benchmarks, with pink, blue and green solid polygons outside the dashed baselines. The right one shows token counts, with the solid polygons well inside the dashed ones. Captions read Avg. +2.1% Better Accuracy and Avg. 44.1% Fewer Tokens. The eye goes first to the radar charts.
caption: SAGE unleashes the efficient reasoning potential of LRMs obscured by pass@1 and identifies the optimal completions within the model's capability hidden in pass@k. By enabling LRMs to learn these efficient reasoning patterns, SAGE-RL-tuned models simultaneously enhance reasoning capacity and conciseness on multiple challenging mathematical benchmarks.
abstract: Recent advancements in large reasoning models (LRMs) have greatly improved their capabilities on complex reasoning tasks through Long Chains of Thought (CoTs). However, this approach often results in substantial redundancy, impairing computational efficiency and causing significant delays in real-time applications. Recent studies show that longer reasoning chains are frequently uncorrelated with correctness and can even be detrimental to accuracy. In a further in-depth analysis of this phenomenon, we surprisingly uncover and empirically verify that LRMs implicitly know the appropriate time to stop thinking, while this capability is obscured by current sampling paradigms. Motivated by this, we introduce SAGE (Self-Aware Guided Efficient Reasoning), a novel sampling paradigm that unleashes this efficient reasoning potential. Furthermore, integrating SAGE as mixed sampling into group-based reinforcement learning (SAGE-RL) enables SAGE-RL to effectively incorporate SAGE-discovered efficient reasoning patterns into standard pass@1 inference, markedly enhancing both the reasoning accuracy and efficiency of LRMs across multiple challenging mathematical benchmarks.
